questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: What a headline foregrounds
questions.learningObjective: say what a headline selects and enlarges when it compresses a report
questions.stem: A headline reads 'Stadt verliert 400 Arbeitsplätze' while the article below it reports the closure of a single factory. What has the headline done to the report?

options.text: It has foregrounded the total and left the single cause out
It has turned a report into a warning about the whole economy
options.misconception: reads a one-line summary as a claim about everything rather than about the article

options.text: It has stated the article's conclusion, since a headline always does
options.misconception: believes a headline is a summary that adds nothing of its own

options.text: It has shortened the report without changing what it claims
options.misconception: assumes compression leaves the claim untouched, which is what a summary should do

questions.explanation: A headline selects one figure, one noun and usually one verb, and everything the report said about limits and qualifications is what gets cut. Option D is what a summary should do and what a headline usually does not, and the test is simple: ask whether the total in the headline could be defended by a reader who has read the whole article, and here it cannot.
questions.hint: Ask what the article claims and what the headline claims, and whether the second is a special case of the first.

questions.topic: The signal a recommendation feed optimises for
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an objective of ranking from the interface text that claims it

options.text: Posts that get a lot of shares move down, so that people reach them first
options.misconception: describes a demotion for a signal, which does not show what the system optimises for

options.text: Posts that readers mark as uninteresting move up, so that they can be corrected
options.misconception: uses the opposite of a like to show a preference, which is not what a like measures

questions.explanation: A ranking system optimises for whatever it measures, so the question is which quantity is doing the work. The first option therefore shows a mismatch between the stated objective and the behaviour: a post rising without a matching rise in likes can only be explained by some other quantity, and length of engagement is the obvious candidate. The fourth confuses a mark of uninterest with a preference, and a system optimising for time would treat that mark as a signal to change, not as a promotion. questions.topic: Mechanism of a filter bubble
questions.learningObjective: describe the feedback loop that produces a filter bubble
questions.stem: Someone reads only one kind of article for a year and then finds other views hard to believe. What has produced that?

options.text: Each click trained the system, so what came next resembled what had already been read
The other views were taken off the internet, so there is nothing left to read
options.misconception: turns a selection effect into a removal of material

options.text: The reader's attention span shortened, so longer arguments became impossible

options.text: The platform paid the reader to read only one kind of article
options.misconception: invents a payment that no such system needs to explain the effect

After a year the reader's experience of the range of available views is a product of the loop rather than of any preference they would now state. Option B mistakes a selection effect for a deletion; the other views are still being published and are still reachable. Option C is a real phenomenon but it is a consequence here rather than a cause, and it does not explain why the same person sees a narrower range than a neighbour. Option D is unnecessary, because no payment is needed to produce the loop once the incentive to predict engagement is in place.

questions.topic: What counts as the second factor
questions.learningObjective: place a second authentication factor into one of the three categories
questions.stem: A banking app asks for a six-digit code sent to the phone that is already logged in. Which category does that code belong to?

options.text: Something the user has, since the code reaches a device rather than a memory
Something the user knows, since the code was issued to the account
options.misconception: classifies a delivered code as remembered knowledge, which is the wrong category

options.text: Something the user is, since holding the phone proves who the user is
options.misconception: treats a device as a biometric factor rather than as a possession

options.text: Something the user can do, since typing a code counts as an action
options.misconception: invents a fourth category, since the standard set has three

questions.explanation: Second-factor authentication rests on three categories: something the user knows, such as a password; something the user has, such as a key fob or a device; and something the user is, such as a fingerprint. A code delivered to a phone sits in the second, because what proves the request comes from the legitimate user is the presence of that device and not the user's memory. Option B is the confusion worth naming, since a code can feel like a password, but the person using it cannot recall it in advance. Option C is the near miss, because possession of a device is not the same as a biometric, and unlocking the phone is in any case a separate step. Option D invents a category; the standard set has three, and the third is the physical characteristic, not the physical action. questions.learningObjective: explain why a longer password resists guessing better than a short complicated one

options.text: The longer one, because it is built from two words a dictionary already knows
options.misconception: reads the presence of dictionary words as an advantage rather than a liability

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: How a false claim keeps spreading
questions.learningObjective: describe the mechanism that keeps a false claim circulating and why correction does not stop it
questions.stem: A claim is demonstrably false and yet keeps circulating, and nobody is repeating it deliberately. What keeps it moving, and why does an official correction so often fail?

answer.exemplar: The mechanism is repetition. A claim that has been seen is more readily believed the second time and more readily passed on, and a repetition arriving from somebody known is harder to check than one arriving from a stranger. Repetition is also cheap for the sender and expensive to answer, since a correction has to be produced, distributed and then believed against the original. That is why an official denial published once loses to a claim repeated a hundred times. Correcting does not always stop it, for four reasons. The correction travels along the same network as the claim but usually with less energy, because few people forward a correction who would have forwarded the claim. A reader who has already repeated the claim has a stake in it and treats the correction as an attack on that. The correction is normally read as a competing claim about the same event rather than as an answer to the particular version the reader saw. And the correction, however accurate, is shorter and duller than the claim, so it loses the competition for attention. What does work is repetition of the correction in the same channels and in the same format, which is why fact-checking services are publications rather than one-off statements.

questions.explanation: The mechanism is repetition, and it has two halves that are usually run together. The first is that a claim which has already been seen is more readily believed the next time and more readily passed on, so the belief is produced by the exposure rather than by the content. The second is that forwarding is cheap for the sender and answering is expensive, since a correction has to be written, distributed and then believed against something the reader has already forwarded. The second half explains the asymmetry that makes official responses useless: a denial published once loses to a claim published a hundred times by a hundred people. Three further reasons make the failure predictable. The correction travels through the same network but with less energy, because few people forward a correction who would have forwarded the claim. A reader who has already repeated the claim now has a stake in it. And a correction is normally read as a competing claim about the same event rather than as an answer to the version the reader actually saw.
questions.hint: Ask what the sender pays to repeat the claim and what the sender of a correction has to pay.

options.text: Ein Analyst hat die Zahlen ausgewertet und nennt ein ähnliches Ergebnis.
options.misconception: makes a reinterpretation the most direct evidence, when it is one step removed from the figures

options.text: Eine Sprecherin des Betriebsrats hat gestern gesagt, die Zahlen seien geschönt.
options.misconception: puts a comment on record behind the figures, when a statement about figures is closer to them

options.text: Der Vorstand hat die Zahlen heute mitgeteilt.
options.misconception: ends with the source closest to the numbers, though it belongs at the start

options.text: Ein Bericht in einer Fachzeitschrift hat die Messwerte veröffentlicht.
options.misconception: places a published measurement behind a named speaker, though a measurement sits nearer the event

The works council's speaker comments on those figures, which adds one step and puts her second. An analyst's reading of the figures is the furthest of the four, because two things now have to be trusted: the figures and the interpretation. questions.learningObjective: state exactly what follows from a comparison of two figures
questions.stem: A claim says 'Seit 2010 sind die Zahlen unverändert.' A fact-check finds the figure for 2010 and the figure for this year. What can it conclude?

options.misconception: turns a verdict about a claim into a rule about what may be quoted

options.misconception: adds a claim about knowledge, which no comparison can establish

options.text: That the figure for 2010 was the wrong one, since the two do not agree
options.misconception: makes a disagreement of two figures into a verdict on the older one

Option C is the commonest overreach in this area, because knowing and asserting are different acts, and a comparison of two numbers says nothing about the state of mind of whoever published the first. questions.topic: What a livestream adds to a recording
questions.learningObjective: name the feature a livestream has that a recorded video does not
questions.stem: A format is described as 'Beim Stream schreiben die Zuschauer während der Übertragung in den Chat.' What does that format make possible that a recorded video does not?

options.text: Commenting on the content while it is happening, so the speaker can answer
Watching at twice the speed, since the material is not bound to a clock
options.misconception: describes a property of recorded material rather than a live one

options.text: Going back a few moments to check what was said, since the text stays available
options.misconception: describes a function of a recording rather than of a live transmission

options.text: Watching without a connection, since the file is stored on the server
options.misconception: invents an offline advantage that a live transmission does not have

questions.explanation: A livestream is a broadcast with a return channel, and the return channel is the whole difference. Because viewers can write while the transmission runs, the event becomes a two-way one, and a speaker can read the room, correct a mistake mid-sentence and take a question. A recorded video has no such channel, and the three wrong options describe things a recording does better: recorded material is not tied to a clock, so it can be watched faster, and it can be rewound, which a live transmission cannot do at all. The last option has the direction exactly backwards, since a live transmission needs a working connection and a recording can be downloaded. The convention that follows from the return channel is that a live show is less scripted than a recorded one, because a speaker who is answering questions cannot predict what will be asked, and that difference is visible to viewers.
questions.hint: Ask what viewers can do to the speaker that they could not do with a recording.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A claim contradicted by the interface around it
questions.learningObjective: answer a privacy slogan with the behaviour of the page that carries it
questions.stem: A platform's page says 'Deine Aufmerksamkeit gehört dir. Wir verkaufen keine Daten.' Yet the site asks for a birth date before showing a film, and that film then disappears from the list. What does the design do to the claim, and what should the page say instead?

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the claim has three parts, and the design contradicts two of them. Selling data is denied, and a request for a birth date followed by the removal of one title from a list is a use of what was given, whether or not a sale followed. Attention belonging to the user is asserted, and a form placed between the reader and the thing they came for takes some of it by force. The third part of the claim, that nothing is asked, is contradicted by the form itself. Stage two: 'Für diese Auswahl fragen wir nach dem Alter. Ohne Angabe sehen Sie den Katalog ohne Empfehlungen.' is the expected version, because it names the field, gives the reason, states the consequence of refusing, and leaves the content reachable either way. What must survive is the fact that a birth date was requested and that something changed in the list afterwards, since a rewrite which only promises good faith has not answered the evidence in front of it. A learner meeting this pattern should look for the request and for the change in what is served, because those two together are the argument a slogan cannot make.

questions.explanation: The design answers both halves of the claim, and the answers are the ordinary ones. A birth date is data about a person, and using it to change what is shown is a use of that data whether or not a sale follows, so the second half of the slogan is contradicted by the page's own behaviour rather than by a court. A form that stands between the reader and the thing they came for takes attention by force, which contradicts the first half. A rewrite has to be about the mechanism rather than about trust, because trust is what the reader has already been asked for and has no reason to supply twice. It should say which field is wanted, why, and what happens if it is not given, and it should let a reader get to the content without answering. Two mistakes are common here: a rewrite that only repeats the promise, and a rewrite that condemns the platform and leaves the reader with no idea what to do next.
questions.hint: List the separate claims in the slogan, then check each one against what the page actually did.

questions.topic: Conventions of a spoken format
questions.learningObjective: name the convention a podcast uses to manage a listener who may be doing something else
questions.stem: A programme's opening runs 'Wir beginnen mit einer kurzen Einleitung und einer Werbeeinblendung, danach folgt das Gespräch.' Which convention is being described?

options.text: A spoken frame in the first minutes that tells the listener what is about to happen
A written summary that the listener reads before pressing play
options.misconception: puts the material in a channel the medium does not use

options.text: A closing address in which the hosts thank the guest by name
options.misconception: replaces an opening convention with one that belongs to the end

options.text: A rating request sent out to listeners after three episodes
options.misconception: moves a request for a review out of the audio and into a separate message

questions.explanation: A podcast is usually heard while the listener is doing something else, and its conventions exist to compensate for that. The opening frame tells a half-attentive listener what has just happened and what is coming, so an episode that is joined halfway is still comprehensible. The advertisement placed inside the programme rather than before it is a further convention, since a listener who wants the content does not have to sit through a preamble to reach it. The credits then go at the end, where a listener who has stayed to the finish will hear them. The wrong options each move a real element of the medium into the wrong place or the wrong channel: there is no written summary to read first, the thanks belongs at the end, and a rating request is an action outside the audio. questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The constraint a video call runs into
questions.learningObjective: name the resource a lagging call has run short of
questions.stem: On a call the picture keeps stuttering and the people talk over each other. What has run out, and what would not help?

options.text: The available time for processing, and a shorter route or a smaller picture would help
The goodwill of the participants, since a technical fault is not a social one
options.misconception: blames the people for a shortage that is in the connection

options.text: The recording capacity, since nothing in a live call is being stored
options.misconception: treats the cause as a shortage of a function the call does not use

options.text: The number of participants, since two people never need more than one line
options.misconception: offers a limit the symptom does not depend on

questions.explanation: The symptom has a technical name. Latency is the delay between a sound leaving somebody's mouth and being heard, and once it passes roughly a hundred and fifty milliseconds a conversation stops being simultaneous and becomes turn-taking, which is what the overlapping shows; a picture that stutters is the same shortage seen in the other channel. Both are solved by reducing the work: a shorter route to the other end, less to send, or a smaller picture to encode. Option B is the reflex of a person who has seen a meeting go badly and reaches for an explanation about the people, and it is the wrong register, since nothing about goodwill changes a packet's journey. Option C names a function a live call does not use, so its level cannot be the constraint. Option D offers a limit the symptom does not mention, and two people can stutter just as badly as twelve.
questions.hint: Ask what the delay is between the two ends, and then ask what could be made smaller.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Using a Sprichwort in a new sentence
questions.learningObjective: fit a German saying into a sentence of one's own and say what the saying contributes
questions.stem: Rewrite 'Ich spare jeden Pfennig, aber das neue Auto passt nicht ins Budget.' with a German Sprichwort, and say what the saying adds to the sentence.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the sentence makes a statement about money and contains no judgement, so it reads as a private calculation that nobody else is expected to accept. Stage two: 'Der Geizige hält sein Geld so fest, dass er sich kein Auto leisten kann.' is a version that works, and the choice of Geizige carries the judgement the plain sentence withheld, since it names the person and not the behaviour. The verb of holding money too tightly gives the mechanism, and dass ... nicht gives the consequence inside a subordinate clause with the verb at the end. What the saying adds is tone and position rather than information: the numbers are already in the original, and a Sprichwort lets a speaker hold a view with a shared image instead of an assertion, which is also why it is easier to disagree with. Three cautions. The saying has to be one the listener knows, since a rare one is less clear than none. The literal sense need not be true. And the register is speech and informal writing, so a Sprichwort in a certificate or an academic sentence is out of place however good the fit.

questions.explanation: A Sprichwort is a complete saying with a message, unlike a Redewendung which is a fixed image without one, and the choice has to fit the sense rather than merely sound apt. The original sentence makes a statement about money and contains no judgement of the kind a saying carries, so the useful addition is the tone: a speaker who reaches for a saying is holding a position with a shared image and not merely reporting a calculation. Three cautions apply, and each one is a real trap. The saying has to be one the listener knows, because a rare saying is less clear than no saying at all, and a learner who has met four of them is at a disadvantage. The literal sense of a saying need not be true, which is a feature rather than a problem. And the register is speech and informal writing, so a Sprichwort in a certificate or an academic sentence is out of place, however apt the sense.
questions.hint: Choose a saying whose message matches the judgement, not just its subject, and check its register.

questions.topic: The weakest source in a report
questions.learningObjective: locate the claim in a report that a reader is least able to check
questions.stem: A report builds its case on a named official, an unnamed passer-by and a study it does not name. Where is that report weakest?

options.text: At the study, since a claim the reader cannot look up is doing the most work
At the official, since a named person is always weaker than a document
options.misconception: reverses the ranking, since a named source can be held to what it said

options.text: At the passer-by, since an eyewitness is the strongest kind of source there is
options.misconception: treats proximity as reliability, which are two different things

options.text: Nowhere, since three sources of different kinds is already enough
options.misconception: counts sources without asking whether any of them can be checked

questions.explanation: A report is as strong as the weakest claim it needs the reader to accept, and the three sources here are not of one kind. A named official can be quoted and held to what was said, and a reader can look for the other statements. A passer-by who is unnamed can be described, so the reader knows the testimony is anonymous even if the report does not say so. An unnamed study can be checked by nobody at all, and it is carrying the weight of the argument, which makes it the weakest link in a chain that looks solid. Option B has the ranking the wrong way round, since a named source is easier to hold to account than an unnamed document. Option C mistakes proximity for reliability: an eyewitness is close to the event and may still be wrong, which is a question about the account rather than about the standpoint. Option D counts instead of weighing, and three sources of different quality are not equivalent to three sources.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three claims a reader could not check without contacting somebody.

questions.topic: Comparing two second factors
questions.learningObjective: compare two second factors by category and by how they travel
questions.stem: A service offers two ways of confirming a sign-in: 'Einmalcode per SMS' and 'Code aus der App'. Which comparison is right?

options.text: Both are possession factors, and the app code is harder to intercept because it never travels
The SMS code is a knowledge factor, since the user reads it before typing it
options.misconception: classifies a delivered code as remembered knowledge

options.text: Both are knowledge factors, since the user has to know the six digits in advance
options.misconception: claims knowledge of digits nobody knows before they are sent

options.text: The app code is the stronger one because it asks the user to do something
options.misconception: invents a fourth category out of the fact that a code is typed

A code sent as a text travels over the mobile network, which means it can be delivered to the wrong number, forwarded by whoever receives it, or taken by somebody who has got hold of the number itself. The two weakest categories to rely on are a code sent by text and a code sent by mail.
questions.hint: Ask whether the code ever leaves the device, and which category the two share.

And it is stable, because it depends on no platform feature and so does not go out of date when the interface changes. What the rule leaves is the other half of the question, and the useful addition is a second clause requiring permission as well, since the two together are what the rule is asking for. A date is worth requiring with the citation too, because a source without a date cannot be checked.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Accurate claims about passwords
questions.learningObjective: separate sound advice about passwords from three widely repeated but wrong rules
questions.stem: Someone is giving advice about passwords. Which of these five statements is accurate?

options.text: A long passphrase resists guessing better than a short string of symbols
A password should be changed every month whether or not it has leaked
options.misconception: prescribes routine rotation, which mainly produces predictable variants

options.text: A password used once and then replaced by a new one is secure on every account
options.misconception: assumes one change protects accounts where the same password is reused

options.text: Writing a password on paper at home is more dangerous than reusing a strong one
options.misconception: overstates a risk a person can manage and understates the cost of reuse

options.text: Once a password is long enough, the characters it contains matter less than its length
options.misconception: also true, because every extra character multiplies the work of guessing

questions.explanation: Two of the five are sound and they are the same fact seen twice. A guesser works outwards from short and obvious candidates, so every extra character lengthens the search, and a passphrase of ordinary words is long without being hard to hold in one's head. Once the length is comfortable, adding a symbol widens the alphabet by very little and is not worth the trouble it causes in use, which is the second correct statement. The three wrong ones are the widely repeated rules rather than the widely observed facts. Monthly rotation produces a series of predictable variants rather than new secrets, and it is the wrong response to a leak, which calls for a change immediately. Changing a password on one account says nothing about the accounts that share it. And a password written on paper at home is a risk a person can weigh and manage, whereas a password reused across four accounts turns one leak into four, which is the larger problem by a wide margin.
questions.hint: Ask how many guesses a character adds, and which of the three rules protects anything at all.

options.misconception: starts with the least permanent item, so a compromised account stays open through the rest of the work

options.text: Der Standort wird auf 'Nur beim Benutzen' gesetzt.
options.misconception: sets the location before the network is protected, so the new setting travels over the old one

options.misconception: protects the local network before the accounts, which can be reached from anywhere

questions.hint: Ask which of the four exposures is still a problem next year if it is left alone.

The name of the authority, which the text supplies in full
options.misconception: treats a detail the article keeps as the thing the headline dropped

options.misconception: names something the reader can find elsewhere, so nothing is really lost

options.text: The type of files, which the headline would not have room for
options.misconception: blames a lack of space for an omission that the article would need as well

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Rewriting a headline that enlarges
questions.learningObjective: restate a headline in German so that it does not claim more than the article supports
questions.stem: A headline reads 'Stadt verliert 400 Arbeitsplätze' for an article about the closure of one factory. Rewrite the headline in German so that it does not enlarge the article.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the headline overstates in three ways. The subject is raised from one factory to Stadt, so a single closure becomes a city-wide figure, which is the enlargement. The verb of losing states the change as a plain fact with no period and no source, so the number has nothing to be measured against. And nothing tells the reader where four hundred came from. Stage two: 'Fabrik in Ostheim stellt 400 Mitarbeiter ein' is the expected version, because it names the actor, the number and the kind of loss in one line without claiming anything the article does not support. '400 Stellen betroffen' is a shorter alternative that keeps the neutrality, and adding 'laut Betrieb' names the source of the figure. What must survive is the number, the loss, and the fact that it concerns employment. A rewrite that softens the wording while keeping Stadt as the subject has not worked, and a rewrite that adds a qualifier to the end of the original is worse, because it invites the reader to discount the number instead of the framing.

questions.explanation: Three things in the headline overstate, and each has to be undone separately. The subject is raised from one factory to the city, which is the enlargement itself. The verb of losing presents the change as a plain fact with no scale and no period, so the number has nothing to be measured against. And nothing marks the figure as what it is, an estimate or a count from one employer. questions.hint: Ask who loses what, and add a word for the source of the figure.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Why a clip is harder to check than a document
questions.learningObjective: explain the asymmetry between verifying a claim about a text and a claim about a recording
questions.stem: Why is a generated clip harder to establish as false than a document claim is to check? What does the difference come from?

answer.exemplar: A document claim leaves traces that exist independently of the claim: a publication date, a file history, a register, a signature, a record of where a version appeared. All of them can be examined by somebody with no access to the author's intent, which is what makes a document checkable. A generated clip leaves almost nothing independent, because the content and the evidence are the same object. Both ordinary checks fail for that reason. Re-encoding removes the mark that records how a file was produced, so the absence of a mark is no evidence of anything. And a viewer cannot read the face, because generated faces and voices have reached the point where the ordinary eye has no usable signal. Verification therefore moves to specialists and to side channels: whether the blinking matches the speech, whether the jaw edge behaves, whether the reflections in the eyes agree with the room, and whether the file's own history shows an editing program. A phone recording with an original timestamp and a witness in the frame is worth a great deal more than a forwarded clip. The consequence for a reader is symmetrical: a clip is not refuted by suspicion, and it is not confirmed by plausibility.

questions.explanation: The difference is where the evidence sits. A document claim leaves traces that exist independently of the claim: a publication date, a file history, a register of circulation, a signature, and any of these can be examined by somebody with no knowledge of what the author intended. A generated clip leaves almost nothing independent, because the content and the evidence are the same object. The two usual checks both fail for that reason. Re-encoding removes the mark that records how a file was made, so the absence of a mark is no evidence of anything at all. And a viewer cannot read the face, because a generated face and a generated voice now sit at the point where the ordinary eye has no usable signal. Verification therefore moves to specialists and to side channels: watching whether the blink pattern matches the audio, looking at the jaw line and the reflections, checking the light against the room, and following the provenance of the file rather than its content. The consequence for a reader is symmetrical and worth stating: a clip is not refuted by suspicion, and it is not confirmed by plausibility.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence exists that does not come from the file's own content.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Accurate claims about what a service learns
questions.learningObjective: separate two sound statements about data collection from three common overstatements
questions.stem: Someone describes what a free service can learn about a reader. Which of these five statements is accurate?

options.text: The service can learn what is watched without any field being filled in
A cookie is the same thing as a fingerprint of the device
options.misconception: puts two different techniques into one word and so describes neither accurately

options.text: Anonymised data cannot be linked back to a person in any way at all
options.misconception: claims an absolute, where the whole question is how hard the link is

options.text: Nothing is collected from a reader who has refused the permission
options.misconception: assumes a refusal reaches every part of a service

options.text: A signed-in session usually provides more than an anonymous visit
options.misconception: also true, since being known is the resource a service is built on

questions.explanation: Two of the five are sound. A service learns from what is watched as well as from what is typed, so a reader who has filled in nothing has still left a record, and this is the point that makes data collection feel invisible. A signed-in session gives a service more than an anonymous visit, since it connects the record to a name, which is exactly the resource a service is built on. The three wrong statements each overstate in a different direction. A cookie and a device fingerprint are different techniques: a cookie is a small file the site asks the browser to return, while a fingerprint is a profile assembled from properties of the browser and the device. Anonymised data is a claim about a process, and the question is always how difficult re-identification is rather than whether it is possible. And a refusal reaches the one thing it was asked about, while the rest of a service continues to observe what happens on the page.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader did not type, and what a refusal was actually about.

questions.topic: A property a live broadcast does not have
questions.learningObjective: identify the assumption in a statement that confuses a live event with a stored file
questions.stem: A viewer says a livestream is better 'weil man auch danach noch zuschauen kann.' What does that statement assume?

That the stream is shorter, since live material is usually brief
options.misconception: invents a difference in length to explain a difference in access

options.text: That the stream is free, since watching costs nothing either way
options.misconception: draws a conclusion about price out of a statement about availability

options.text: That the stream is edited, since editing happens while the show runs
options.misconception: assumes live material is corrected in flight, which is rare and unannounced

questions.explanation: The statement moves a property of one format onto another. A live transmission exists at the moment it runs, and watching it afterwards means watching a recording of it, which is a different artefact with different properties: it can be paused, cut, searched, and watched at a different speed. So the ability to return to a stream is not evidence that it is a livestream, and a viewer who values that ability is describing a preference for recordings. Option D is the reverse of the usual assumption, since live material is normally unedited and the absence of edits is one of its features. The two formats answer the two questions differently, and it is worth keeping them apart when reading about a platform.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence describes the moment of the broadcast or the file it leaves behind.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Who can still find material after it has been deleted
questions.learningObjective: name the copies a deletion by the writer cannot reach
questions.stem: A user has removed every post and emptied the caches they know how to find. Who can still get at the material?

options.text: A reader who took a screenshot, an archive that collected the page, and a search index
Nobody, since the caches were the only remaining copies
options.misconception: assumes the user's own device held every copy that existed

options.text: Only the platform, because it owns the copy it has removed
options.misconception: gives ownership of a copy that somebody else took

options.text: Only an administrator with a court order, which no reader could produce
options.misconception: leaves out the readers and archives that already hold it

questions.explanation: A deletion by the writer reaches the writer's copies, and the material survives wherever somebody else took one. A reader who screenshotted it has a copy that no command from the writer can touch. An archive that collected the page keeps its own copy by design, since that is its purpose, and it is usually not reachable by a request from the person who posted. A search index holds a reference to material it cannot display, and that reference is enough to find a copy elsewhere. The other three all assume that one party held everything, and each names a different single party. It is worth being precise about the platform, since it does hold a copy and can remove it, which is what the user did. Being able to delete something is not the same as being the only person who has it, and that gap is the whole of the notion of a footprint.
questions.hint: Ask who made a copy, and which of those people can be reached by a delete button.

questions.learningObjective: test a claim about the reader's control against what the page does to the reader's attention
questions.stem: A platform says it gives people control, and the page places a large button in the middle of the screen that returns every article to the top. What does that do to the claim?

options.misconception: turns a consistent annoyance into evidence of quality

options.misconception: treats visibility as candour, which are different things

options.text: It has nothing to do with the claim, since a claim about control is about permissions
options.misconception: separates attention from control, which are the same question in this sentence

Option C mistakes visibility for candour, and a platform that is open about what it does with the button has still spent the attention. questions.stem: A learner is told that the sentence 'Ich fahre morgen mit dem ICE nach Basel' contains an error. What is wrong with that judgement?

options.misconception: requires a formality that written German has never demanded of a name

options.misconception: asks for a German ending on a name that has none

options.text: The verb should be in the past, since travel plans are reported in the past
options.misconception: mistakes a plan for an event that has already happened

The verb is in the present because the sentence reports a plan, and the present is what German uses for a fixed future. The other three options each ask for something the language does not do. This is the shape of a common error in marking, where a fluent sentence is corrected for a feature that is actually a choice, and the useful response is to ask which rule is being applied and where it is written down.

questions.learningObjective: name the norm a silent participant breaks and the signal that would satisfy it
questions.stem: In a video meeting someone joins with the camera off for an hour and says nothing. Which norm has been broken?

options.misconception: describes a different fault altogether

Formal clothes are a matter of the workplace rather than of the norm, and a room in which somebody is quietly taking notes is not the problem. The last option is simply a different fault, and the fault here is silence.

questions.learningObjective: set out the three abilities in a plan for digital education and what it leaves unstated

answer.exemplar: The phrase normally names three abilities and leaves the largest part to somebody else. Medienkompetenz covers judging a source, a claim and a post, and it is the ability that survives a change of platform, since the tools change and the questions do not. The second is any statement about checking whether the plan works, and that is the difference between a list of intentions and a programme.
